full_note_paragraphs: Jesus answers Peter’s refusal with οὐκ ἔχεις μέρος μετʼ ἐμοῦ, which WEB renders “you have no part with me.”
The noun μέρος can refer to a part, share, or portion. In this context, “no share with me” brings out participation with Jesus more clearly than “no part.”
Receiving Jesus’ washing is therefore presented as necessary for sharing with him. The phrase doesn’t, by itself, define every theological dimension of that participation.
interpretive_limits: The phrase doesn’t identify every theological dimension of Peter’s participation with Jesus.
It doesn’t by itself establish one final interpretation of baptism, regeneration, or continuing forgiveness.
annotations.short_note: WEB says Peter would have “no part” with Jesus unless Jesus washed him. Greek μέρος can mean a part, share, or portion. “No share with me” makes the language of participation and belonging easier to hear.

full_note_paragraphs: WEB says that someone who has “bathed” only needs the feet “washed.” Greek uses λελουμένος, from λούω, for the bath and νίπτω for washing the feet.
The wording distinguishes a whole bath from a local washing. The perfect participle identifies the person as already bathed, while the footwashing remains a separate act.
The lexical contrast is clear. The verse doesn’t by itself decide whether the bath represents baptism, initial cleansing, regeneration, or another theological category.
interpretive_limits: The two verbs don’t settle a complete sacramental theology.
The separate textual variant involving “except the feet” isn’t part of this bounded issue.
The perfect form shouldn’t be made to carry more theology than the discourse supports.
annotations.short_note: John 13:10 uses two Greek verbs. λούω refers to bathing, while νίπτω refers here to washing the feet. Translations that use “wash” for both can hide the contrast.

full_note_paragraphs: The Greek clause ends ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι. There is no separate Greek word corresponding to the English pronoun “he.”
English often supplies “he” because “that I am” sounds incomplete. The addition clarifies the immediate claim that Jesus is the one he has said he is.
Leaving the phrase as “I am” makes John’s repeated wording easier to see. Possible resonance with the divine name belongs to the wider Gospel and isn’t proved by the supplied pronoun alone.
interpretive_limits: Supplying “he” is a normal English clarification, not evidence that the translator changed Jesus’ identity claim.
The grammar alone doesn’t prove a direct quotation of Exodus 3:14.
The immediate context emphasizes Jesus’ foreknowledge so that the disciples may believe when the prediction occurs.
annotations.short_note: WEB says “I am he,” but Greek reads ἐγώ εἰμι, “I am,” without a separate word for “he.” English supplies “he” to complete the identification. That clarification also makes John’s repeated wording less visible.

claim_summaries.claim_summary: The bound WEB verse says “you have no part with me.”
Greek μέρος can denote a part, share, or portion.
In this context, “no share with me” makes relational participation more explicit without settling its complete theological meaning.
The bound WEB verse distinguishes “bathed” from “washed.”
The Greek uses λελουμένος from λούω for the bath and νίπτω for washing the feet.
Using one English verb for both actions can conceal the Greek lexical contrast.
The bound WEB verse contains the English phrase “I am he.”
The Greek reads ἐγώ εἰμι without a separate word corresponding to “he.”
The supplied pronoun clarifies the immediate identification while making John’s repeated “I am” wording less visible.
